newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN probe suspects 134 massacres by Kabila's troops.
newsitem.headline: UN probe suspects 134 massacres by Kabila's troops.

text.p: A U.N. human rights investigator said he received information on about 134 incidents of massacres of Rwandan refugees in the former Zaire carried out by forces loyal to President Laurent Kabila, according to a report released on Friday.

The report, by Robert Garreton of Chile, said future investigators should ask "whether a genocide was planned and executed" and whether the perpetrators should be brought before an international tribunal.
It also said serious human rights violations and killings continued in the new Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Garreton, a respected human rights lawyer, has been denied further entry to the country by Kabila's government after his earlier report that cited 40 massacre sites.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan this week said he would organise the investigation himself, without Garreton, so it could be undertaken quickly.
Garreton's new, harsher report for the U.N. Human Rights Commission, completed on July 2, was based on interviews in May with survivors in Rwanda as well as U.N. staff.
The new report did not estimate how many people were killed or give a precise total of the number of separate massacres, which are believed to be over 190.

But Garreton said that 68 percent or 134 of the allegations received were traced to rebels loyal to Kabila and his Tutsi allies. The remainder were committed by the former Zairean army under ousted President Mobuto Sese Seko or Rwandan Hutu militia that controlled the refugee camps.
"Many testimonies mentioned the unbearable stench from mass graves almost everywhere in Kivu," in the eastern part of the country, he said.

"According to the information received, several thousand people were killed, including large numbers of women and children," Garreton said, adding that tens of thousands of others disappeared into forests where many probably died of malnutrition and disease.

"The methods used," he said, were "deliberate, premeditated massacres, the dispersal of refugees to inaccessible inhospitable areas, the systematic blockade of humanitarian assistance and the stubborn opposition thus far to any attempt to conduct an impartial objective investigation into the very seriously allegations."

Over a million Hutus in 1994 crossed into what was then Zaire fearing reprisals for the genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners. The bulk returned home, but U.N. relief officials say up to 200,000 remain unaccounted.
Garreton said he was equally concerned at persistent allegations of human rights violations and massacres, particularly in the Kivu area, and at the "violent suppression of mass demonstrations."

"In this connection, the summary executions, which accompanied the seizure of power in Kinshasa, bear out concerns about the action of (Kabila's) soldiers out of the range of the cameras and raise worrying questions about their future role in a society that is supposedly making the transition to democracy."

The report noted that the long-term causes of the conflict were colonial frontiers drawn regardless of borders recognised by ethnic groups and aggravated by transplanting populations and then the enormous influx of Rwandan refugees.
